opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a question I think about a lot, partly because my own work has gone back and forth on it.

My honest view is that architecture matters, but probably less than people assumed ten years ago, and in a different way. Early in deep learning, architecture was the main lever. Going from AlexNet to VGG to ResNet, or the DenseNet work I was involved in, each design change gave real accuracy gains, because we were still figuring out basic things like how to make very deep networks trainable at all. Residual connections and normalization made a huge difference.

Once those basics were solved, a lot of the "architecture gap" turned out to be a training-recipe gap. That was part of the motivation behind ConvNeXt. When Vision Transformers came out and beat ConvNets, people concluded attention was fundamentally better for vision. But when we took a standard ResNet and modernized it step by step, using the same training techniques, data augmentation, larger kernels, and macro design choices that transformers had benefited from, the pure ConvNet could match or beat Swin Transformers. So a big share of what looked like an architecture advantage was really about data, optimization, and scale.

So today I'd say the dominant factors for making AI useful are data, compute, and the training pipeline, and architecture is more of an enabler. A good architecture is one that scales gracefully, is efficient on the hardware we have, and doesn't get in the way. The transformer won largely because it's simple, general, and maps well onto GPUs, not because it's uniquely intelligent.

That said, I don't think architecture research is finished. Where it matters most now is efficiency and capabilities the current designs handle poorly: long context, memory, inference cost, and running models on smaller devices. If you can get the same quality at a tenth of the compute, that makes AI far more useful and accessible, even if benchmark accuracy doesn't change. So my advice to students is to hold architectural claims to a high standard, control for the training recipe, and focus on changes that alter scaling behavior or cost, not just a point on a leaderboard.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Ravid. I think architecture matters, but maybe not in the way people used to assume. For a long time, the field treated architecture as the main lever. Every year there was a new backbone, and we thought that was where progress came from. My own view, which came partly out of the ConvNeXt work, is that a lot of the apparent gains from new architectures were really gains from training recipes, data, and scale. When we took a plain ResNet and modernized the training procedure and a handful of design choices, it closed most of the gap with Vision Transformers. So the architecture was not the magic ingredient people thought it was.

That said, I would not say architecture is unimportant. It is just that its importance has shifted. What matters now is less about squeezing out another point of accuracy and more about properties like scalability, how well the model handles different modalities, how efficiently it runs on actual hardware, and how easy it is to train stably. Transformers won largely because they are simple, general, and scale predictably, not because attention is uniquely expressive. If you want AI to be useful, those practical properties end up mattering more than cleverness.

The other thing I would emphasize is that usefulness is increasingly determined after pretraining. The architecture sets the ceiling, but data, post-training, and how the model is deployed decide how much of that ceiling you actually reach. So when a student asks me whether they should work on architecture, I tell them it is still a good problem, but they should think about it in terms of systems and scaling, and be honest about baselines. Many architecture papers compare against a weak baseline, and the improvement disappears when you tune the old model properly. That lesson has been true for a long time, and it is still true today.

astra-6.text:
I think architecture is important, but its importance depends on what you’re trying to improve. If you want better accuracy, architecture is one piece alongside data, compute, and the training recipe. It’s easy to attribute a gain to a new architecture when some of it actually comes from how the model was trained. So I think careful comparisons are really important.

For making AI more useful, architecture also affects things like inference speed, memory usage, and how easily a model can run on the hardware people have. Two models might achieve similar accuracy, but if one is much cheaper to deploy, that can make a big difference in practice.

I’m particularly interested in how far we can get with simple designs. A more complicated architecture isn’t necessarily a better one. Sometimes revisiting an existing design and making a few well-motivated changes gives you a very strong model. So I’d assess architecture by what it enables under real constraints, rather than just whether it produces a higher benchmark score.

sol-6.1.text:
I think architecture is important, but its importance depends on what you mean by useful. If you want the best performance with a fixed amount of compute, architecture can make a real difference. It determines how efficiently you can train a model, how much memory it needs, and how quickly you can run it. Those things affect who can actually use the model.

At the same time, architecture is one part of a larger system. The data, the training objective, and the amount of compute also matter a lot. When we compare two architectures, we have to be careful that we're not really comparing two different training recipes or different levels of engineering effort.

So I tend to value simple architectures that are easy to train and scale. A new architectural idea is especially compelling when it gives us a capability or an efficiency improvement that we couldn't get just by tuning the existing model better. For making AI useful, that practical benefit matters more than architectural novelty by itself.
